claims.text: The initial W–Cu composite contains W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix.
The untreated W–Cu composite typically exhibits phase separation.
The untreated W–Cu composite typically contains interfacial voids.
High-temperature solid-state diffusion bonding at 1000–1080 °C can be applied without melting Cu.
The proposed diffusion-bonding treatment should be conducted under moderate pressure and an inert atmosphere.
Diffusion bonding enhances interfacial bonding at W–Cu interfaces.
Diffusion bonding reduces voids at W–Cu interfaces.
Atomic diffusion and improved wetting are responsible for enhanced W–Cu interfacial bonding and reduced void formation.
Diffusion bonding promotes atomic intermixing between the W and Cu phases.
Diffusion bonding reduces phase separation in the W–Cu composite.
Eliminating interfacial voids and improving W–Cu bonding improves thermal contact between the W and Cu phases.
Improved thermal contact between W and Cu increases the effective thermal conductivity of the composite.
The diffusion-bonded composite will have measurably higher thermal conductivity than the untreated composite under relevant heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
The intervention is applicable only when the starting composite has sufficient W–Cu interfacial contact.
The intervention is limited by Cu thermal stability, excessive grain growth, and the need to avoid melting.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity improvement depends on the initial microstructure and diffusion-bonding parameters.
There is no direct evidence supplied for the post-bonding irradiation stability of the treated composite.
